title: Citizen of the world
hookLine: asked where he came from, Diogenes said he was a citizen of the world (Diogenes Laërtius 6.63)
carry: a bigger home around the smaller one

lines: OURS AND THEIRS IN TWO SECONDS.
cards: Where are you from? It's the first question at a party, on a form, at a border, and the answer sorts people into ours and theirs in about two seconds.
Now picture a scruffy old man in the market in Athens, the one who told Alexander the Great to stand out of his sunlight. Somebody asks him where he's from.
He could say Sinope, the town on the Black Sea where he was born, and which threw him out. Instead he gives an answer nobody had given before. Today: kosmopolitēs.

teach.b: Diogenes Laërtius reports that when Diogenes the Cynic was asked where he came from, he said: I am a citizen of the world. In Greek, kosmopolitēs: kosmos, the ordered universe, plus politēs, citizen of a polis, a city.

It's the first time we find the word, and it's the root of our cosmopolitan. Remember, Diogenes wasn't a Stoic. He was a Cynic, like Crates, the man Zeno followed out of a bookshop back on day twenty-six.
But the Stoics took the idea and made it central. In a Greek world where your city was your identity, your law, your gods and your army, saying my city is the world was almost shocking.
Epictetus told his students not to answer I'm an Athenian or I'm a Corinthian, but to think of themselves as citizens of the whole.
Seneca said each of us belongs to two communities: the small one we happen to be born into, and the great one that holds gods and humans together.

teach.h: ROME AS ANTONINUS, THE WORLD AS HUMAN.
teach.b: And Marcus Aurelius, who was actually running an empire, wrote something like this: as Antoninus, my city is Rome; as a human being, it's the world. He didn't give up Rome.
He kept both. That's the Stoic version: not no home, but a bigger home around the smaller one. It's yesterday's outermost circle, taken seriously, as if the people there were your neighbors too.

how: People drawn to Stoic cosmopolitanism keep their local loyalties while trying to treat people everywhere as fellow citizens of one human community.

o: a stylish person who has traveled to many cities
a citizen of the whole world, not just one city
a person who has lost or given up their homeland

games.q: the world city — tap the pairs.
p: first said citizen of the world
Rome as Antoninus, the world as human

s: the phrase citizen of the world began with the Stoics
Diogenes the Cynic said it first; the Stoics took it up.
Marcus Aurelius gave up Rome for the world
he kept both: Rome as Antoninus, the world as a human being.
Seneca spoke of belonging to two communities
the one you're born into, and the great one holding all.

games.q: you're Diogenes, exiled from Sinope. someone in Athens asks where you're from. what do you say?
o: I am a citizen of the world.
games.why: he answered kosmopolitēs, the first time the word appears, and the root of our cosmopolitan.

practice: Picture the place you'd name if someone asked where you're from: its streets, its weather, its food, and let that be home.

Then let the picture widen, the country around it, the ocean past that, a city on the other side of the world where someone is waking up as you breathe. Hold both, the small home and the big one, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Kosmopolitēs. Greek for citizen of the world: Diogenes' answer to where are you from, taken up by the Stoics.

orig.note: Greek: citizen of the world, from kosmos and politēs.

carryVoice: Your line: a bigger home around the smaller one. Rome as Antoninus, the world as a human being. Until tomorrow.

sources.work: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers
